review_output.summary: The rented ArrayPool<int> buffer is not returned inside try/finally, so any exception between Rent and Return leaks it.
review_output.failure_scenario: A purpose contains a lone surrogate (e.g. "\uD800"). SecureUtf8Encoding.GetByteCount throws EncoderFallbackException at line 370, so Return at line 397 never runs. A caller that keeps retrying CreateProtector with bad input drains the pool, and each failed call falls back to a fresh allocation. The old MemoryStream path had no pooled resource to leak.

review_output.summary: The total AAD length is summed with unchecked int arithmetic. On overflow it wraps instead of throwing, which the old MemoryStream path would have done.
review_output.failure_scenario: Purposes whose combined UTF-8 byte count exceeds int.MaxValue make totalPurposeLen wrap to a negative or small value. The result is OverflowException at `new byte[]` or an ArgumentOutOfRange/IndexOutOfRange from Slice/GetBytes, not a clear error. The old code went through checked((int)...) and MemoryStream's capacity checks.

review_output.summary: The new path is gated on `#if NET10_0_OR_GREATER`, but every API it uses exists on any NETCOREAPP target, and this file already uses `#if NETCOREAPP` at lines 144 and 297.
review_output.failure_scenario: It is inconsistent with the rest of the file. If the default TFM is ever multi-targeted with an older netcoreapp, that build silently falls back to the slow MemoryStream path. Use `#if NETCOREAPP` to match the existing guards.

review_output.summary: The AAD serialization now exists twice (span-based for net10, BinaryWriter for netfx/netstandard2.0), and no test checks that the two produce identical bytes.
review_output.failure_scenario: The AAD is part of the authenticated-encryption contract. If a later edit to one branch makes the bytes differ, payloads protected on net10 will not unprotect on net462/netstandard2.0, and vice versa. A simpler option is one span-based implementation for all TFMs, since BinaryPrimitives and ArrayPool are available via System.Memory/System.Buffers on netstandard2.0. The only TFM-specific piece would be LeadingZeroCount, which a loop can replace.

review_output.summary: No test exercises the new hand-written 7-bit length encoder with multi-byte lengths or non-ASCII purposes. Existing tests only use short ASCII purposes.
review_output.failure_scenario: An off-by-one in Measure7BitEncodedUIntLength or Write7BitEncodedInt at the 127/128 or 16383/16384 byte boundaries, or with multi-byte UTF-8 characters, would change the AAD bytes. That silently breaks unprotection of existing payloads, and the suite would not catch it. Add tests with a 128+ byte purpose and a non-ASCII purpose, comparing against BinaryWriter output.

review_output.summary: Renting an int[] from ArrayPool just to cache per-purpose byte counts adds complexity, and it is the only reason a try/finally is needed.
review_output.failure_scenario: Purpose arrays are tiny (usually 1-5 entries). A simpler, allocation-free form is `Span<int> lengths = purposes.Length <= 16 ? stackalloc int[16] : new int[purposes.Length];`. Calling GetByteCount again in the second loop would also work. Either way the Rent/Return bookkeeping and the leak risk go away.

review_output.summary: `using System.Buffers.Text;` is never used. The new usings are also out of order: System.Buffers.Binary comes before System.Buffers, and System.Buffers.Text sits after the Microsoft.* usings.
review_output.failure_scenario: On netstandard2.0/net462, where none of these usings are needed, the unused directive raises IDE0005/CS8019 warnings, which may fail builds that treat warnings as errors. It also adds noise and violates the repo's sorted-using convention.

review_output.summary: A commented-out loop is left as dead code after a return statement in Measure7BitEncodedUIntLength. The magic numbers 4 and `4 + keySize + 4` are used instead of sizeof(uint), and the variable totalPurposeLen actually holds the total AAD length.
review_output.failure_scenario: This makes maintenance harder. The dead code below the return is misleading, and the hard-coded offsets duplicate layout knowledge that GetAadForKey expresses as sizeof(uint)/sizeof(Guid). If the header layout changes, those offsets can drift out of sync.
